draft.title: Costs and benefits for different groups
card: One decision can affect different groups in different ways. A group can gain from it while another group loses.
Four groups to look at are consumers (people who buy), workers (people who are employed), businesses (owners and sellers) and government.
Weigh the effects on each group separately. A benefit to one group does not cancel out a cost to another.
Example: a council lets a large supermarket open in a town. Shoppers may get lower prices, and some local shops may lose customers.
draft.remember: Ask who gains and who loses, one group at a time.

a.q: A council lets a large supermarket open in a small town. Shoppers pay less, but nearby shops lose sales. What does this show?
opts: The decision helps one group and costs another
The decision helps every group in the town
The decision has no effect on any group
The decision only affects the local council
a.why: Shoppers are consumers who gain from lower prices, and the nearby shops are businesses that lose sales. Different groups are affected in different ways. It is wrong to say every group gains, because the shops lose.
a.clue: Look at what happens to shoppers and to nearby shops.

b.q: Mia runs a café in Dubbo. She cuts her staff's hours to save money. Which group bears a cost from this decision?
opts: Workers, who earn less pay
Consumers, who pay higher prices
Government, which must close the café
Businesses, which lose all their income
b.why: Fewer hours means workers are paid for less time, so they bear a cost. Mia's business saves money, so it gains rather than loses. Nothing in the case says prices rise or that the government acts.
b.clue: Who is paid for the hours that were cut?

a.best: The decision helps one group and costs another

problems.detail: The distractor 'The decision only affects the local council' uses 'only', an absolute word the card does not use. Absolute distractors are easy to rule out without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'Government, which must close the café' uses 'must', and 'Businesses, which lose all their income' is also absolute. A student can rule these out on wording alone.

check.summary: Both questions are correct and match the card and the explanations. A few wrong options use absolute words ('only', 'must', 'all'), which makes them easy to rule out.

proposal.title: Costs and benefits for different groups
card: One decision can affect different groups in different ways. A group can gain from it while another group loses.
Four groups to look at are consumers (people who buy), workers (people who are employed), businesses (owners and sellers) and government.
Weigh the effects on each group separately. A benefit to one group does not cancel out a cost to another.
Example: a council lets a large supermarket open in a town. Shoppers may get lower prices, and some local shops may lose customers.
proposal.remember: Ask who gains and who loses, one group at a time.

a.q: A new mine opens near a town. Locals get jobs there, but renters in the town face higher rents. How should you weigh this decision?
opts: Look at the effects on workers and renters separately
Treat the workers' gain as cancelling the renters' cost
Count the effect on workers, as more people gain jobs
Count the effect on renters, as costs matter more than gains
a.why: Each group is weighed on its own, so the gain to workers and the cost to renters are both kept in view. The gain to workers does not cancel out the cost to renters, so treating one as making up for the other is wrong.
a.clue: Can one group's gain make up for another group's loss?

b.q: Mia runs a café in Dubbo. She cuts her staff's hours to save money. Which group bears a cost from this decision?
opts: Workers, who are paid for fewer hours
Consumers, who pay more for their coffee
Government, which pays the café's staff wages
Businesses, as the café spends more on wages
b.why: Fewer hours means workers are paid for less time, so they bear a cost. Mia's business spends less on wages, so it saves money rather than losing it. Nothing in the case says prices rise, and the government does not pay the staff.
b.clue: Who is paid for the hours that were cut?

a.best: Look at the effects on workers and renters separately

b.best: Workers, who are paid for fewer hours
